sentences.text: Arkansaurus was a bipedal dinosaur that measured about 4.6 meters long and weighed approximately 380.5 kilograms.
This animal likely possessed long arms ending in three hands with claws on the fingers.

Its feet featured strongly curved claws that bent downwards, a distinct trait among ornithomimosaurians which typically have flat claws, and unique anatomical features including differentiated toe bone bases and a distal ungual phalanx with a very weak flexor tubercle.
The holotype foot revealed a greenstick fracture, the first such record among dinosaur fossils, along with evidence of a potential gout.
Arkansaurus was officially designated as the state dinosaur of Arkansas in 2017.
Arkansaurus fossils were first noticed by Joe B. Friday in August 1972 when he saw vultures circling his land in Locksburg, Arkansas.
Friday collected the bones and displayed them at his gas station for several months before paleontologist Dr. James H. Quinn identified them as dinosaur fossils and prepared them for study.
The original bones were donated by Joe B. Friday and now reside at the University of Arkansas Museum Collections.
The known fossil record of Arkansaurus consists of three metatarsals, four phalanges, and three claws.

Daniel Chure initially promised to name the fossils but was unable to do so at that time, so Angela K. Braden formally published the full species name Arkansaurus fridayi in 1998, noting that James H. Quinn had used the name informally earlier, while the official scientific description was published on March 19, 2018, in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology by ReBecca Hunt-Foster and posthumously by James H. Quinn.
Arkansaurus was likely a fast-moving omnivore.
ReBecca Hunt noted similarities between the Arkansaurus foot and footprints found in the Glen Rose Formation of Texas and the Moenave Formation of Utah.

Arkansaurus is classified in the Ornithomimosauria in a basal position, outside of the Ornithomimidae family, and as an ornithomimosaur, it is a rare representative of the Early Cretaceous group in North America, more closely related to Nedcolbertia than to contemporary Asian forms.
Arkansaurus lived during the Aptian and Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 113.2 to 100.5 million years ago.
It lived in what is now North America.
It is debated whether Arkansaurus lost its first toe or if the absence is due to fossilization processes.
Some researchers suspected the fossils were a forgery, but this hypothesis was quickly refuted by experts.
In 2002 and 2003, ReBecca Hunt-Foster suggested Arkansaurus might be a separate taxon related to Ornitholestes, but concluded the fossil remains did not justify its formal designation.
